My wife and daughter were away at Girl Scout camp this weekend, so my 10-year-old son and I took the opportunity to take a road trip. He got the idea of going to the [Franklin Institute](https://www.fi.edu/) in Philadelphia.

Even though we live in the Metro NYC area, Philly is only a bit more than an hour and half drive away. It's one of the perks of living in the East Coast Megalopolis. We left around 8am on Saturday morning, hit a bit of Shore Traffic (it being Memorial Day Weekend after all), and got to downtown Philly around 9:40. After parking we walked to the museum, and arrived pretty much exactly at 10:00am when it opened.

The first thing you see when you enter the museum is the Benjamin Franklin National Memorial. It's an enormous statue of the seated Franklin, reminiscent of the Lincoln Memorial in Washington. Fitting, since Franklin was a titan of reason.

Past that is the regular museum entrance. We were disappointed that the coupons we clipped for a discount on admission were not valid if we wanted to see any of the special exhibits. It's always annoying when coupons are so narrowly focused that you can't use them. We paid \$46 for admission and the special exhibit, which seems like a lot but is the going rate for museums these days. Plus with the amount of time we spent there we got our money's worth.

We happened to be there on the first day of this special exhibit, about [Numbers in Nature](https://www.fi.edu/exhibit/mirror-maze-numbers-nature). They highlighed three types of patterns: the golden ratio, fractals, and [Voronoi diagrams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voronoi_diagram). I knew a lot about the first two but very little about the third. Given a set of points in the plane, the plane can be partitioned into cells determined by the closest point. For instance, the arrangement of popcorn kernels around the cob form a Voronoi pattern.

The “fun” part of that exhibit was a mirror maze. On a triangular lattice they laid out a maze, and the walls of the maze were mirrors. When I was a kid and I followed my mom on shopping trips, I remember the department stores had these triptych mirrors so that you could see yourself from several angles while trying on the clothes. The three mirror panels were all the same rectangular shape, and the outer panels were hinged. My brother and I loved to close the mirrors in on ourselves, so that they formed an equilateral triangle. When you do this, each mirror reflects the other two, and each of those is reflecting the other two, and so on to triangular infinity. This maze was the same thing, except that some of the surfaces were mirrored, and others were actually passages through the maze. It was extremely disorienting, in a fun way. You couldn't tell how far “forward” extended before you hit a wall. I bumped my nose more than once. The only clue I found was to look for fingerprints on the mirrors. It took us two tries—the first time we came out at the entrance—but we finally got through the maze.

The permanent exhibits of the Franklin Institute were also very enjoyable. The heart exhibit is one of their oldest continuous exhibit, and it shows a bit. The highlight is a giant fiberglass heart that you can walk through, up the vena cava, into the right atrium and ventricle, through the lungs, back to the heart through the pulmonary vein, into the left atrium and ventricle, and finally out the aorta. Too bad this was designed only for the ambulatory. I think it would be impossible to build something like this is in the ADA era. Virtual reality is a nice technological workaround for that, and in fact the FI had several VR exhibits.

We also spent a long time in the flight exhibit. I may have finally gotten a bit of understanding into Bernoulli's principle: faster moving area has lower pressure. So a ball can balance on a column of forced air, buoyed up by the air. But more than that, the pressure differential between the column of moving air and the surrounding “stationary” air pushes the ball back towards the column, creating a stable equilibrium.

The same principle gives wings their lift. Air moves more quickly across the curved top of the wing than the flat lower surface. This speed differential again creates a pressure differential, which pushes the wing up. The rest of flight is moving foward fast enough to create enough lift.

After seeing nearly every exhibit, and taking in a planetarium show, we left the museum after more than six hours. So like I said, we got the most out of our admission price. We had planned to visit the Liberty Bell after, but it was in the opposite direction from the car, and we were all walked out. So we left, but not without a trip to Dallessandros for cheesesteaks.

I've only had the pleasure of a Philly Cheesesteak in Philly a couple of times. But I have to concede that they do it best there. Certain varieties of wine have controlled names that only can be used if the wine comes from that place. For instance, only sparkling white wines from the Champagne region of France can be called *champagne*. The notion is that there's something unique about the land where it comes from (*terroir*) that makes the wine spacial. So it is with the cheesesteak. I think only the ones served within metropolitan Philadelphia should bear the appellation.

We got to Dal's right before a big rush. There were only a few people in line and the counter was nearly empty. We opted for a seat at the counter since it was air conditioned inside. Good idea, but poorly executed. We took the seats closest to the ordering counter, which meant that when the rush came, people were crowding behind us, shouting orders between our shoulders. There is also the option to sit outside, or take it to go. I might opt for outside next time.

I ordered my cheesesteak with American cheese (as recommended by the server), and “fried” (more like sautéed, but that's what they called them) onions. It didn't need anything more than that. At the table, they had some spicy, vinegary hot peppers that were good for cutting the grease and brightening the palate. My son ordered his with provolone and pepperoni, because that's what he usually puts on his sandwiches at home. I noticed a lot of folks in line were ordering extra cheese, or two cheeses, such as American and Cheez Whiz (one might argue that neither of those is a cheese, but then one may be tempted to order swiss cheese instead, thus dooming one's presidential campaign).

The sandwiches are about a foot long. My son's first bites were tentative, as he tried to pick the whole thing up and eat it hot dog-style. I showed him the crosscut in the middle so that it can be broken into two halves, and how, once divided, you eat from the large end towards the small end of each half. *These are the lessons a boy needs a father for.*

[View this photo on Instagram](https://instagram.com/p/BUnZoGWjnyN)

He got about five bites in before he announced he was full. Not me. I ate every bit of mine. The server wrapped his up with a smile and we were on our way. We were home less than two hours later.

Now that we've done the Franklin Institute and gotten a little of the lay of the land, I'm hoping we can go back to Philly and see the Liberty Bell, Independence Hall, and all that jazz. I also would like to take in some of their art museums. And I think Dal's is going to be the regular last stop from now on.
